newsitem.title: INDIA: India coffee exporters seek rules to curb defaults.
newsitem.headline: India coffee exporters seek rules to curb defaults.

text.p: Indian coffee exporters, worried by the rising number of international contract cancellations, have appealed for regulatory standards to prevent defaults, a top exporter said on Monday.
Coffee Exporters' Association president Ramesh Raja said the liberalisation of India's coffee trade had brought about changes which would be positive in the long-run.

"But in the short run, there would be certain teething problems, which we are already facing. Some defaults in international contracts have already taken place," Raja told Reuters in an interview in this southern Indian town.
Raja said the cancellations amounted to nearly 3,600 tonnes of coffee, which had been contracted earlier but cancelled by exporters who ended up paying a "penalty" to buyers.
Earlier this month, India freed the coffee trade, allowing growers to directly market all their produce after five decades of controls.
Until recently, growers holding more than 10 hectares of coffee land had to surrender 30 percent of their produce to the state-run Coffee Board for marketing.
Raja said the Coffee Board now had no marketing role and as a third party it could represent the interests of all concerned -- growers, traders and exporters.
"The Coffee Exporters' Association has suggested to the Coffee Board that it move from controls to one of regulation," he said.
Raja said the coffee trade needed a watchdog agency such as the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), which regulates the country's stockmarkets.
"The Coffee Board could evolve itself into a forum for arbitration," he said.
Raja said there had been cases of growers not delivering contracted quantities in anticipation of a rise in prices when the market turned volatile.

"Second, you have quality problems, where coffee contained extraneous matter and then you have bunching of arrivals into the market or no arrivals at all, as growers held back their inventories," he said.
Raja said intermediaries between growers and exporters also played a large role, often bidding up prices to artificial levels, causing severe price distortions in the market.
"All these factors have led to the cancellation of several contracts," he said. "People do not like cancellation of contracts. The shipper (exporter) gets tagged as unreliable.
"In the last one month, buyers have been paid compensation by exporters, which is in reality a penalty."
Indian coffee exports rose to 153,000 tonnes in 1995-96 (April-March) from 137,400 in the previous year, their value rising to 13.70 billion rupees ($380 million) from 11 billion in the same period.
